title: In Chennai, Deepavali Shopping That Puts Tamil Nadu's Women Makers First
excerpt: At the Mathi Experience Store in Nungambakkam, festive sweets, handloom textiles and gifts are made by women self-help groups from districts across Tamil Nadu — and every purchase helps keep those groups in business
body:
• The Mathi Experience Store in Nungambakkam, Chennai, sells only products made by women self-help groups from across Tamil Nadu.
  • Run by the Tamil Nadu Corporation for Development of Women under the Mahalir Thittam, the store stocks Deepavali sweets and savouries alongside handloom textiles, handicrafts, spices and millet-based foods.
  • Products are quality-checked at production sites before they reach the shelves, and are reordered on the basis of demand.
  • An adjoining cafe serves tea, coffee, milkshakes and snacks, making the store a place to slow down as well as shop.

As Deepavali shopping gathers pace in Chennai, one address is asking customers to think about who made what they are buying. The Mathi Experience Store, on Valluvarkottam High Road in Nungambakkam, sells products made by women self-help groups (SHGs) from districts across Tamil Nadu. A purchase there, the reasoning goes, does more than fill a festive basket — it helps an underprivileged woman build a livelihood of her own.

The store stands next to Valluvar Kottam, in the Anna Teresa Women's Complex. Its glass walls show the shelves to passers-by before they step inside, and inside, according to the report, the layout itself makes a point: the shelves replicate the map of Tamil Nadu, with each district represented by what its women produce.

A store laid out like a map of Tamil Nadu

Traditional printed table runners from Udhagamandalam sit beside mud pots and tea cups from Viluppuram. Traditional musical instruments from Thiruvallur, bamboo combs and toothbrushes from Kancheepuram, paintings from Thanjavur and showpieces from Nagapattinam fill other sections. Beyond those district specialities, the assortment includes handloom textiles, handicrafts, spices, soaps and body care products, millet-based foods and other food items, sanitary napkins and eco-friendly products.

The Mathi brand itself was created to give those products a market. As Women Entrepreneurs Review has reported, the brand was born of an effort by Tamil Nadu minister Udhayanidhi Stalin to promote items from women's SHGs, with the government establishing an e-commerce platform and the first Mathi shop in Chennai to support SHGs as they became producer collectives.

How products reach the shelves

The store was started by the Tamil Nadu Corporation for Development of Women (TNCDW) under the Mahalir Thittam and was established in 2023. Five women currently manage it in shifts, most of them from SHGs themselves, and the staff includes a woman with hearing and speech disabilities. The store has kept a record of its progress from the beginning; employee M. Mahalakshmi showed the register's first entry, made by Udhayanidhi Stalin — the MLA for Chepauk-Thiruvallikeni — on the day he inaugurated the outlet.

Onboarding is deliberate rather than open-ended. Groups approach district officials to register under the Mahalir Thittam, officials visit production sites to assess products and quality before anything is selected for display, and products are reordered on the basis of demand. "Everything in the store is organic and comes after quality checks," Mahalakshmi said.

Food first for Deepavali, and a cafe to slow down in

For food shoppers, the seasonal draw is the festive table. As Deepavali approaches, the shelves make room for traditional festive delicacies prepared by SHGs — sweets and savoury packs that, Mahalakshmi said, are generally in demand, with the festival specials usually arriving a few days before Deepavali. Millet-based foods and spices offer a longer-lasting way to stock a pantry from the same makers.

Mathi is not only a shop. An adjoining cafe serves tea, coffee and cappuccino, along with milkshakes and snacks, with outdoor seating away from the bustle of the city.

For diaspora families visiting Chennai for the festival, the store offers a single stop where festive food, handloom and craft all trace back to named districts — and to the women who made them.
